newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banker calls for probe into closed accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banker calls for probe into closed accounts.

text.p: The head of the Swiss Bankers Association has called for a probe into thousands of dormant passbook savings accounts closed by Swiss banks without their owners' knowledge after World War Two.

Records uncovered recently in cantonal archives in Lausanne listing names of account holders and their savings now worth millions of dollars have fuelled controversy over the wartime role of Swiss banks, accused by critics of being clearing houses for plundered Nazi gold and of hoarding the money of Jews.

Industry association chief Georg Krayer, a critic of the way banks have handled the crisis, said the passbook accounts -- which do not technically qualify as bank accounts -- might prove to be a loophole in the search for Holocaust victims' funds.

He said they had to be probed by an independent commission that is already searching bank files for lost accounts. Swiss banks and Jewish groups agreed last May to set up the panel, headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Paul Volcker.
He said the panel should also look into other cantons in Switzerland to find out what happened with similar passbooks.

"The commission must investigate these accounts. If not, I will raise the question myself. Otherwise this is going to become a loophole everyone will jump on," he said on Thursday at a dinner hosted by his association.
"You have to go through all the lists to see if there were meaningful figures."
Krayer said his association could publish the lists of passbook holders on its Internet web site.
In Zurich, the Swiss National Bank (SNB), reported it had found only a small number of unclaimed private assets on its own books as it pores over its records.

"These efforts have led to the discovery of only a small number of accounts and safe deposit boxes which were maintained at the SNB and which might be remotely connected with the topical issue of dormant assets," it said.
The SNB, the Swiss central bank, held only a small number of private accounts, and the practice ended in the last decade.

The records Krayer referred to belonged to Lausanne's Credit Foncier Vaudois Bank, which was taken over by Banque Cantonale Vaudoise, Switzerland's fifth biggest bank. They list thousands of people, mainly Swiss but including many foreigners.
They may open the way to fresh claims against Swiss banks which have repeatedly stated that they were missing many, if not all, of their archives and documents about old accounts.

The money from accounts closed after banks lost contact with the owners was often donated to charities, and it appears the banks made little effort to find the owners of accounts being slated for closure.

Swiss banks have to keep documents for 10 years after bank accounts are closed. But the government last year banned banks from destroying any documents that could help the search for Holocaust victims' wealth.
After a year of arguing with Jewish groups, Swiss banks acknowledged in February they held 39 million Swiss francs in dormant funds, some of which might stem from Holocaust victims.
But the World Jewish Congress (WJC) rejected the sum as too small, saying there may be billions of dollars more. Banks insist they have acted properly.
Krayer said he did not expect investigations to uncover large sums, mainly because Jews appeared to have deposited a lot of money in the name of intermediaries.

"The money wasn't meant to be in the names of people it belonged to. Jewish business people were quite shrewd. Would you think you would go into a bank in Switzerland with a Jewish name during the Nazi days? This was not a safe place to go," he said.
"But the storm is not over yet," he added. "The Volcker commission will raise a lot of questions that will stay open, which will simply be impossible to find out."
